(IV) ARGUMENTS:-
a) Ld. Counsel for IP no.10 argued that the LAC has sent a sum of Rs.1,19,939.98/- in respect of award no.2237 whereby 33 bigha 16 biswas of land was acquired.
The acquired land was purchased jointly by Sh. Budh Ram and Sh. Radha Krishan and they approached the Revenue Authorities for mutation of the same.
However, the acquired land could not be mutated due to objection raised by Custodian, Evacuee Property as Sh. Budh Ram and Sh. Radha Krishan had only 17/64 share in the same.

Thereafter, they appointed one Sh. Sewak Ram by way of Power of Attorney to look after the their legal proceedings and he had illegally transferred the said land to Sh. Qabul Singh (IP no.7) on 15.07.1954 by way of sale deed.

It is further argued that the said land got mutated in the name of Sh.
Qabul Singh vide mutation no.795 in the revenue record.
b) Thereafter, Sh. Budh Ram challenged the validity of the said mutation by filing application before the Revenue Assistant and First appeal before the Additional Collector.
Both of them got dismissed.

Aggrieved, they approached the Ld. Judicial Secretary, who has vide order dated 31.05.1969 set aside the LAC No.73/16 Union of India Vs. Abdul Wahid Pg No. 17 of 28 dismissal of above said application and appeal and held that Sewak Ram had no right to sell the land in question to IP no.7 and the mutation is liable to be dismissed.

Therefore, only LRs of IP no.10- Buddh Ram had pursued the case and led the evidence which requires appreciation.

b) At the outset, it is pertinent to mention herein that after filing of the instant reference petition,

sentences.text: On perusal of the claim petition, it is observed that the same is vague and does not specify the land regarding which claim has been sought.
Further, the entire claim petition revolves around the change of mutation on account of judgment of Judicial Secretary dated 31.05.1969.

However, whether the said mutation pertains to the land in dispute in the instant petition or not, cannot be ascertained as neither the said mutation was tendered in evidence nor any supporting evidence led in this regard.
Thus, the entire claim petition is silent on the aspect of identity of the land regarding which claim has been preferred.

c) Further though, IP no.10 has filed the instant claim petition in respect of 1/4th share in the total land acquired, but the reference pertains only to Khasra nos.540/52, 541/52, 542/52, 188 min, 189,
190, 191, 192 and 193, as specified in the particulars of dispute mentioned in the memorandum referred to this Court U/s 30-31, L.A. Act, which warrants adjudication in the instant petition.

Therefore, the claim of the IP no.10 in respect of the remaining acquired land cannot be entertained by this Court as being the reference Court, this Court cannot go beyond the scope of reference forwarded to it for adjudication.

Since the present reference pertains only to the land bearing Khasra nos.540/52, 541/52, 542/52, 188 min, 189, 190, 191, 192 and 193, the claim of the IP no.10 in respect of remaining land stands rejected being beyond the purview of the reference in question.

Reliance in this regard can be placed upon the case titled as 'Sharda Devi Vs. State of Bihar & Anr.'
dated 08.01.2003 wherein while quoting 'Nusserwanjee Pestonjee Vs. LAC No.73/16 Union of India Vs. Abdul Wahid Pg No. 19 of 28 Meer Mynoodeen Khan Wullud Meer Sudroodeen Khan Bahadoor,
6 Moo Ind App134', it is so held:-
"Their Lordships of the Privy Council have held that wherever jurisdiction is given by a Statute and such jurisdiction is only given upon certain specified terms contained therein it is a universal principle that those terms should be complied with, in order to create and raise the jurisdiction, and if they are not complied with the jurisdiction does not arise.
Further, In Kothamasu Kanakarathamma and Ors. Vs. State of Andhra Pradesh and Ors. AIR 1965 SC 304, this Court held that under the Land Acquisition Act the matter goes to the Court only upon a reference made by the Collector and there is no doubt that the jurisdiction of the Court arises solely on the basis of a reference made to it.
The Court can adjudicate upon the matter referred to it but the Court is certainly not invested with the jurisdiction to consider a matter not directly connected with it and Union Of India vs Abdul Wahid on 13 May, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/199284839/

sentences.text: this is not a matter of mere technicality.
A case of lack of inherent jurisdiction will not be cured by mere failure to object to the proceedings before the Court on the ground of an absence of reference on matters not referred.
There can be no waiver or acquiescence.

Indeed, when there is an absence of inherent jurisdiction, the defect cannot be waived nor can be cured by acquiescence".
d) Further, the jurisdiction of the Reference Court, vis--vis "persons interested" has been explained by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Shyamali Das v. Illa Chowdhry & Ors., AIR 2007 SC 215, holding that the Reference Court does not have the jurisdiction to entertain any application of pro interesse suo, or in the nature thereof.

sentences.text:
The Court held as under:
"The Act is a complete code by itself.
It provides for remedies not only to those whose lands have been acquired but also to those who claim the awarded amount or any apportionment thereof.
A Land Acquisition Judge derives its jurisdiction from the order of reference.
It is bound thereby.
His jurisdiction is to determine adequacy and otherwise of the amount LAC No.73/16 Union of India Vs. Abdul Wahid Pg No. 20 of 28 of compensation paid under the award made by the Collector".

"It is not within his domain to entertain any application of pro interesse suo or in the nature thereof."
e) In Ajjam Linganna & Ors. v. Land Acquisition Officer, RDO, Nizamabad & Ors., (2002) 9 SCC 426, the Hon'ble Supreme Court made observations to the effect that it is not open to the parties to apply directly to the Reference Court for impleadment, and to seek enhancement under Section 18 for compensation.
In Prayag Upnivesh Awas Evam Nirman Sahkari Samiti Ltd. v. Allahabad Vikas Pradhikaran & Anr.,
(2003) 5 SCC 561, this Court held as under:
"It is well established that the Reference Court gets jurisdiction only if the matter is referred to it under Section 18 or Section 30 of the Act by the Land Acquisition Officer and if the Civil Court has got the jurisdiction and authority only to decide the objections referred to it.

Further, though, IP no.10 is recorded as -  for the relevant year of 1947-48 in respect of the entire land in dispute, however, no supporting evidence such as proof of rent paid or revenue receipt with the concerned authority has been placed on record.
Rather in Column no.10 under the heading pertaining to Revenue () it categorically records " " (without rent/ revenue).
Apart from Jamabandi for the year 1947-48, no record regarding continuation of his tenancy in subsequent years or prior to the year 1947-48 has been placed on record.

Further, neither the subsequent Jamabandis nor any record reflecting possession of the IP no.10 over the land in question at the time of notification U/s 4, L.A. Act i.e. 13.11.1959 or at the time of date of award i.e. 28.03.1969 or at the time of possession is placed on record.

h) Further, IP no.10 also relied upon the order of Judicial Secretary-Ex.H2 vide which mutation no.795 recorded in favour of Qabul Singh was cancelled and mutation no.794 recorded in favour of Buddh Ram and Radha Kishan.

However, mere reference regarding change of mutation does not prove the entitlement of the IP no.10 to claim compensation in respect of the land in dispute without leading cogent positive evidence in support of his claim.

Further, even the order of Judicial Secretary Ex.H2 does not specify the particulars of khasra numbers for LAC No.73/16 Union of India Vs. Abdul Wahid Pg No. 24 of 28 which mutation has been recorded.

sentences.text: "The plaintiff came in possession of the suit land some-where in the year 1989.
There is no agreement on the file showing that the plaintiff came in possession of the suit land as a tenant.
There is no receipt about the payment of rent by the plaintiff to the defendant.
The entry of Jamabandi in which the plaintiff has been recorded in possession of the suit land at tenant-at-Will in the Column of cultivation is not sufficient to show has tenancy over this land.
The law is well settled that when a person is in unauthorized occupation of some land, he is generally recorded as tenant at will i.e. gair marusi.
The entry in column of cultivation has to be read with the column of rent so as to determine the status of a person in possession of the land.

sentences.text: Learned trial Court did not consider the legal consequences of the entries in the revenue record and simply relied upon the entry of gair marusi in the column of cultivation to come to a conclusion that the plaintiff was a tenant over the suit land.

sentences.text: As noticed earlier, the meaning of word Gair Marusi is non-occupancy.
In view of these entries, the plaintiffs are not even proved to be tenant on the land.
The word Gair Marusi itself does not imply that the person in occupation is a tenant.
For arriving at conclusion whether a person is tenant or not, the entry in the column of rent has to be carefully read in conjunction with the entry in cultivation column.
In the present case, the entry in the rent column does not show that the plaintiffs were in possession as a tenant under the land owners".
